1.q: A 52-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes has 2 weeks of fatigue and a temperature of 38.4 °C (101.1 °F). She has no known heart disease, does not inject drugs and has no skin, eye or nail findings. Three sets of blood cultures show no growth. Transesophageal echocardiography shows an oscillating mass on the mitral valve. Which modified Duke classification fits?
opts: One major plus three minor needs three minor criteria; she has only fever. Diabetes is not a predisposing heart condition, and she has no vascular or immunologic findings, so she is possible, not definite.

Correct. The oscillating mass on the valve is a major criterion (1), and a fever of 38.0 °C or higher is a minor criterion (1). Her cultures are negative and diabetes is not a listed predisposing heart condition, so she has one major plus one minor: possible endocarditis.

Two major criteria would need positive blood cultures as well as the echocardiogram finding. Her three culture sets show no growth, so she has one major criterion (the mass) and one minor (fever): possible.
ruled out by a stated finding
Three minor criteria would need predisposition, vascular or immunologic findings besides fever, and she has none. Her valve mass is a MAJOR criterion, giving one major plus one minor: possible.

1.q: A 19-year-old basketball player with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with outflow obstruction has a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the left sternal border. He also has seasonal allergies. Which maneuver will make the murmur louder?
opts: Correct. Valsalva lowers preload, and anything that decreases blood flow through the heart increases the outflow obstruction and makes the murmur of obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy louder. Standing, and amyl nitrite through lowered afterload, do the same.
Passive leg raising returns blood to the heart and increases preload, which reduces outflow obstruction and softens the murmur. Lowering preload with Valsalva or standing makes it louder.
Handgrip raises afterload, which reduces the outflow obstruction and decreases the murmur. Valsalva does the opposite by lowering preload, so the murmur becomes louder.
Rapid squatting increases preload, and more blood in the heart reduces outflow obstruction, so the murmur gets softer. Valsalva, which lowers preload, is the maneuver that makes it louder.

1.q: A 76-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation, a permanent pacemaker, chronic kidney disease with reduced renal function and an allergy to iodinated contrast has calf claudication and an ankle-brachial index of 0.6. Which imaging study is most appropriate for her?
opts: Correct. Duplex ultrasound is the mainstay, initial noninvasive imaging when arterial stenosis is suspected, and it needs no contrast or radiation. Each alternative collides with one of her conditions: contrast allergy and reduced renal function rule out computed tomography angiography, and a pacemaker rules out magnetic resonance angiography.

Computed tomography angiography uses contrast to outline arterial anatomy, and its contraindications are contrast allergy and decreased renal function. She has both, so duplex ultrasound is the safe noninvasive study.
ruled out by a stated finding

Conventional angiography is the invasive gold standard, requiring vascular puncture and injected contrast, and it is used mainly to guide a planned intervention. For an initial look in a patient allergic to contrast, duplex ultrasound comes first.
gold standard chosen over first test

Magnetic resonance angiography is the alternative for a patient allergic to contrast, but pacemakers and intracranial aneurysm clips are its contraindications. Her pacemaker rules it out, leaving duplex ultrasound.

1.q: A 68-year-old man who smoked for 40 years and has hypertension and type 2 diabetes has a 3.4 cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm on screening ultrasound. He has no abdominal or back pain. How often should the aneurysm be imaged?
opts: Elective repair in a man is for an aneurysm larger than 5.5 cm or one growing 0.5 cm in six months. A painless 3.4 cm aneurysm needs surveillance with ultrasound every three years.
right action at the wrong stage
Ultrasound or computed tomography every 6 to 12 months is for an aneurysm of 4.0 to 5.4 cm. At 3.4 cm his aneurysm is in the 3.0 to 3.9 cm band, which is imaged every three years.
An abdominal aorta over 3 cm is aneurysmal even at 3.4 cm, and once found an aneurysm gets routine follow-up for size and growth rate. His interval is ultrasound every three years.

Correct. The infrarenal aorta averages 2 cm and over 3 cm is aneurysmal; a 3.0 to 3.9 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm is followed with ultrasound every three years. Surveillance frequency is set by size, so his diabetes, which is linked with a lower risk of aneurysm, does not change it.

opts: Less than 1 g is stricter than the limit taught for dilated cardiomyopathy. The education point is sodium restriction to less than 2 g per day, alongside medication adherence and regular follow-up.

Correct. Patient education in dilated cardiomyopathy includes restricting sodium to less than 2 g per day, together with medication adherence, regular follow-up and removing any offending source such as alcohol or cardiotoxic agents.

Less than 3 g is looser than the limit for dilated cardiomyopathy, which is less than 2 g of sodium per day. The restriction is part of the same education as medication adherence and removing offending sources.
Less than 4 g is twice the allowed amount. Patients with dilated cardiomyopathy are taught to keep sodium below 2 g per day, along with alcohol cessation and adherence to their medication regimen.

Which is the next step?
opts: Magnesium treats polymorphic ventricular tachycardia WITH a prolonged QT (torsades). His QT was normal at 420 ms and he has ischemic chest pain, so he is defibrillated and sent for urgent coronary angiography.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia without a prolonged QT is most commonly due to acute myocardial ischemia, as with his crushing chest pain. Even if the patient looks well, polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never truly stable: defibrillate, then urgent coronary angiography with possible revascularization.

Synchronized cardioversion is for unstable MONOMORPHIC ventricular tachycardia with a pulse. His QRS shapes vary, and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never truly stable, so he is defibrillated even with a pulse.
Procainamide is a pharmacologic option for STABLE MONOMORPHIC ventricular tachycardia. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never truly stable and is treated with defibrillation.

1.q: A 47-year-old woman with hypothyroidism has her third episode of pericarditis. She has stayed on colchicine, but every attempt to taper prednisone has brought a flare (steroid-dependent disease). She has a temperature of 38.4 °C and a C-reactive protein of 42 mg/L (normal under 10). Which therapy is preferred now?
opts: Colchicine is continued for months in recurrent disease (6 months or more), not stopped. Her steroid dependence with fever and a high C-reactive protein calls for anti-interleukin-1 therapy.

Escalating prednisone ignores that she is already steroid-dependent, one of the situations in which anti-interleukin-1 therapy (anakinra or rilonacept) is preferred. Corticosteroids also carry osteoporosis risk.

A nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug is part of first-line therapy for a FIRST episode, and dropping colchicine and steroid support at her third flare would undertreat her. Recurrent, steroid-dependent disease calls for anakinra or rilonacept.

Correct. Current guidance supports anti-interleukin-1 therapy (anakinra or rilonacept) earlier for an inflammatory phenotype (C-reactive protein over 10 mg/L, fever, pericardial inflammation), and it is preferred for recurrent, colchicine-resistant or steroid-dependent disease. She is recurrent, steroid-dependent and inflamed.

1.q: A 31-year-old man had an upper respiratory infection last week. He has sharp substernal chest pain that is worse lying back and eases leaning forward. No pericardial friction rub (a superficial scratchy sound) is heard on repeated examination. His electrocardiogram shows widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression and reciprocal ST depression in aVR. Echocardiography shows no pericardial effusion. How many of the four diagnostic criteria for acute pericarditis does he meet?
opts: One criterion counts only his chest pain. Widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression is the suggestive electrocardiogram criterion, so he meets two of four.

Correct. The four criteria are sharp substernal chest pain, a pericardial friction rub, suggestive electrocardiogram changes (widespread ST elevation) and a new or worsening effusion. He has the chest pain (1) and the electrocardiogram changes (1): 1 + 1 = 2, which meets the two-of-four rule for a clinical diagnosis.
Three would need a friction rub or an effusion as well, and he has neither: no rub on repeated examination and no effusion on echocardiography. He meets two: the pain and the electrocardiogram.
ruled out by a stated finding
Four would need all of pain, rub, electrocardiogram changes and a new effusion. He has no rub and no effusion, so he meets two, which is still enough for the diagnosis.
ruled out by a stated finding

1.q: A 34-year-old man who injects heroin has a temperature of 39.2 °C (102.6 °F) and painless flat red spots on his soles (Janeway lesions). Two separate blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. Transthoracic echocardiography shows no vegetation, and a transesophageal study is pending. Which modified Duke classification fits now?
opts: Two major criteria would need echocardiographic evidence of endocardial involvement as well; his transthoracic study showed no vegetation. His one major (cultures) plus three minor criteria still make it definite.
ruled out by a stated finding
One major plus one minor undercounts him: injection drug use, fever and Janeway lesions are three separate minor criteria. One major with three minor is definite.

Correct. Staphylococcus aureus from two separate blood cultures is one major criterion. Injection drug use (predisposition), fever of 38.0 °C or higher, and Janeway lesions (vascular phenomena) are three minor criteria: 1 major + 3 minor = definite endocarditis, even before the transesophageal study.
Three minor criteria alone give possible endocarditis, but his cultures are a MAJOR criterion (a typical organism in two separate cultures). One major plus three minor is definite.

1.q: A 58-year-old man comes to the emergency department with three days of left calf pain. He is receiving chemotherapy for colon cancer, and he also has hypertension and type 2 diabetes and smokes. His left calf measures 4 cm more than the right 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity, he has pitting edema confined to the left leg, and he is tender along the course of the deep veins. No other diagnosis seems as likely. What is his Wells score for deep vein thrombosis?
opts: A score of 3 leaves out his chemotherapy. Active cancer, meaning treatment or palliation within the past 6 months, earns 1 point, so his total is 4. Both numbers sit in the high band, but only 4 counts every Wells item he actually has.

Correct. Active cancer under treatment 1 + calf swelling more than 3 cm over the other leg 1 + pitting edema confined to the symptomatic leg 1 + tenderness along the deep venous system 1 = 4, which is 3 or greater: high likelihood. Hypertension and smoking are deep vein thrombosis risk factors but not Wells items, and diabetes is not scored either.

A score of 5 adds a point for smoking. Smoking raises the risk of deep vein thrombosis, yet the Wells criteria score only cancer, immobility, the leg findings and an alternative diagnosis, so the correct total is 4.
risk factor counted as a Wells item

A score of 6 scores both smoking and hypertension. Each appears on the deep vein thrombosis risk-factor list, but neither is a Wells item; only his cancer, calf swelling, pitting edema and deep-vein tenderness count, for a total of 4.
risk factor counted as a Wells item

1.q: A 22-year-old man with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy collapsed while running and was resuscitated from ventricular fibrillation. He also has seasonal allergies and anxiety and is now stable on metoprolol. Which is the most appropriate addition to protect him from sudden death?
opts: Surgical myectomy excises part of the septum to relieve outflow obstruction, and mitral regurgitation may resolve with it. His problem is survived ventricular fibrillation, which calls for an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator.

Correct. Sudden cardiac death is the leading cause of death in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and in more than 80% of cases it comes from ventricular fibrillation, which he has already survived. An implantable cardioverter-defibrillator, part of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy management, is placed to treat that rhythm if it returns.

Alcohol septal ablation injects alcohol into septal branches of the left coronary artery to cause a therapeutic infarction that thins the septum over months, relieving outflow obstruction. It does not guard against ventricular fibrillation; a defibrillator does.

Digoxin is a positive inotrope that is avoided in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy because increased contractility raises ischemia risk and may induce arrhythmias. After a ventricular fibrillation arrest he needs an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator.

1.q: A 29-year-old woman who injects heroin and has hepatitis C has tricuspid valve endocarditis. Blood cultures grow methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Which antibiotic fits?
opts: Correct. Staphylococcus aureus causes most endocarditis in people who inject drugs, and 80 to 90% when the tricuspid valve is infected. For the methicillin-RESISTANT strain, the listed agents are vancomycin or daptomycin.
Nafcillin (or oxacillin) treats METHICILLIN-SUSCEPTIBLE Staphylococcus aureus. Her organism is methicillin-resistant, so vancomycin or daptomycin is used.
ruled out by a stated finding
Cefazolin is an option for methicillin-SUSCEPTIBLE Staphylococcus aureus. For her methicillin-resistant strain the agents are vancomycin or daptomycin.
ruled out by a stated finding

Penicillin G (with or without gentamicin) treats viridans streptococci, the classic subacute oral-flora organism. Her tricuspid infection grows methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, treated with vancomycin or daptomycin.

1.q: A 66-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease and diabetes has missed a week of dialysis. He has pleuritic chest pain (sharp, worse with each breath in) and a pericardial friction rub (a superficial scratchy sound). Blood urea nitrogen is 96 mg/dL (normal 7-20). Echocardiography shows a small effusion without tamponade. Which treatment addresses the cause?
opts: Pericardiectomy is considered for constrictive pericarditis, large refractory effusions or frequent symptomatic recurrences. His uremic pericarditis with a small effusion is treated by dialysis.
Correct. A blood urea nitrogen above 60 mg/dL marks uremic pericarditis, and his 96 after a missed week of dialysis fits. Treatment targets the underlying disorder, and for uremia that is dialysis.

Treating tuberculosis addresses tuberculous pericarditis, mainly in developing countries, and can slow constriction. His blood urea nitrogen of 96 after missed dialysis points to uremia, treated with dialysis.

Steroids treat the underlying disorder in AUTOIMMUNE pericarditis. His pericarditis is uremic (blood urea nitrogen 96 after missed dialysis), and the underlying-cause treatment for uremia is dialysis.

1.q: A 71-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, hip osteoarthritis and a 30-pack-year smoking history has pain, numbness and weakness in both thighs when he walks. Standing still does not relieve it; the symptoms ease only when he sits down or leans forward. His pedal pulses are normal. Which is the most likely cause of his leg symptoms?
opts: Osteoarthritis pain is often present at rest and worsened by exercise, and it may improve when weight is taken off the joint. Relief that requires sitting or leaning forward, with numbness and weakness, fits spinal stenosis instead.

Correct. Spinal stenosis causes claudication-like symptoms with numbness and weakness that are relieved by rest AND by sitting down or leaning forward to straighten the lumbar spine. Rest alone relieves true claudication, and his normal pulses argue against arterial disease despite his diabetes and smoking.

Peripheral neuropathy, common in elderly patients with diabetes, gives a continuous burning sensation in the foot that is unaffected by exercise. His thigh symptoms come on with walking and ease with sitting or leaning forward, the pattern of spinal stenosis.

Aortoiliac disease gives buttock, hip and thigh claudication that is relieved by rest, usually within 10 minutes, with diminished femoral pulses. His symptoms need sitting or leaning forward and his pulses are normal, which points to spinal stenosis.

opts: Adding a second diuretic intensifies diuresis, the opposite of the preoperative rule. When pericardiectomy is planned, diuretics are used sparingly.
Aggressive diuresis is what the preoperative rule warns against: if surgery is planned, diuretics are used sparingly. His fluid overload is ultimately relieved by the pericardiectomy.
Fluid boluses are the temporizing measure for cardiac TAMPONADE, to raise preload. He has constriction with anasarca; before surgery his diuretics are continued sparingly, not replaced with fluid.

Correct. Constrictive pericarditis is often a surgical disease, and if surgery is planned, diuretics should be used sparingly in the preoperative period. Diuretics treat fluid overload in early, stable constriction on a medical trial, but heavy preoperative diuresis is avoided.

1.q: A 50-year-old man being evaluated for endocarditis has painful red nodules on his finger pads, painless flat red spots on his soles, conjunctival hemorrhages, and septic pulmonary infarcts on chest imaging. Which finding counts as an immunologic minor criterion?
opts: Septic pulmonary infarcts are vascular phenomena, listed with major arterial emboli and mycotic aneurysm. The immunologic minor criterion here is the painful finger-pad nodules (Osler nodes).

Correct. Painful finger-pad nodules are Osler nodes, and the immunologic minor criterion covers glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots and rheumatoid factor. His other three findings belong to the VASCULAR minor criterion, so together he has two separate minor criteria from these signs.

Painless flat spots on the soles are Janeway lesions, which sit under the VASCULAR phenomena criterion with emboli, infarcts and conjunctival hemorrhages. The immunologic one is the painful finger-pad nodule (Osler node).
Conjunctival hemorrhages are listed under vascular phenomena, not immunologic phenomena. The immunologic finding here is the painful finger-pad nodules (Osler nodes); Roth spots would also qualify.

1.q: A 71-year-old woman with hypertension had a myocardial infarction 3 weeks ago and takes aspirin. She now has fever, sharp pleuritic chest pain (worse with each breath in) that eases leaning forward, and widespread concave ST elevation: Dressler syndrome. A colchicine-based regimen with gastrointestinal protection is planned. Which drug should be avoided?
opts: Correct. Pericarditis weeks after an infarction (Dressler syndrome) is post-infarction pericarditis, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as indomethacin and ibuprofen are not given for it; aspirin is the anti-inflammatory used instead, with colchicine and gastrointestinal protection.

Gastrointestinal protection with a proton pump inhibitor such as omeprazole is recommended with anti-inflammatory therapy, not avoided. The drug to avoid after an infarction is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug such as indomethacin.

Aspirin is the anti-inflammatory that IS used for post-infarction pericarditis, and she already takes it as an antiplatelet. The drug to avoid is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug such as indomethacin.

Colchicine is paired with aspirin or a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug as first-line therapy for most patients and is not one of the drugs avoided after an infarction. The drug to avoid here is the nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug indomethacin.

opts: A permanent pacemaker treats symptomatic bradycardia and high-grade block; it cannot shock a fatal rhythm. After surviving ventricular fibrillation he needs an implantable defibrillator, which senses fatal rhythms and shocks.

Catheter ablation treats premature ventricular contraction-induced cardiomyopathy or refractory symptomatic beats. After a ventricular fibrillation arrest, secondary prevention is an implantable defibrillator.

Correct. Once stabilized after life-threatening ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation, most patients need an implantable cardioverter defibrillator for secondary prevention of sudden cardiac death. Coronary artery disease, as in his prior infarction, is the most common predisposing condition for sudden death.

A beta blocker treats symptomatic premature beats and non-sustained ventricular tachycardia. A survivor of ventricular fibrillation needs an implantable defibrillator for secondary prevention of sudden death.

ruled out by a stated finding
Admit for heparin infusion and warfarin

A filter is reserved for an acute proximal clot with active bleeding or another contraindication to anticoagulation. Kidney disease is not one of those; she can be anticoagulated, starting with unfractionated heparin in the hospital.

Five days of enoxaparin followed by dabigatran is an outpatient regimen, and outpatient care requires no renal insufficiency. With a creatinine clearance under 30 mL/min she is admitted and given an unfractionated heparin infusion instead.

1.q: A 32-year-old man with asthma went hiking 3 weeks ago, had a tick bite and then an expanding red rash. He now feels lightheaded. His electrocardiogram shows Wenckebach block (the PR interval grows longer with each beat until a QRS is dropped). He takes no medications and has no history of heart disease. Which is the most likely cause?
opts: Degenerative conduction disease is a cause of block in old age; he is 32. His recent tick bite and expanding rash make Lyme carditis the cause that fits.
ruled out by a stated finding
Atrioventricular node ischemia after a myocardial infarction is a listed cause, but he is 32 with no heart disease or chest pain. A recent tick bite with an expanding rash points to Lyme carditis.
ruled out by a stated finding
Beta blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and digoxin cause Mobitz type I block, but he takes no medications. The tick bite and rash point to Lyme carditis.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. A PR interval that lengthens until a QRS drops is second-degree Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) block, and Lyme disease (Lyme carditis) is a listed cause. A tick bite and expanding rash 3 weeks before, in a young man on no medications, point to it rather than age-related or ischemic causes.

1.q: A 15-year-old soccer player's father was just diagnosed with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy after fainting. The teen has no symptoms and uses an inhaler for exercise-induced asthma. Which step is most appropriate for the teen?
opts: A defibrillator is placed in select high-risk patients, not in an asymptomatic teen whose diagnosis is not yet established. Screening comes first because the disease is autosomal dominant and his father has it.
right action at the wrong stage

Correct. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is mostly inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, so one affected parent is enough to pass it on, and evaluation is often prompted by disease in a family member. Genetic screening is the care strategy named for adolescents.
Metoprolol is the initial medication for symptomatic outflow tract obstruction. He has no symptoms and no diagnosis yet; with an affected father, he needs screening for the inherited disease first.

Waiting for symptoms is risky because hypertrophic cardiomyopathy may be asymptomatic and is the leading cause of sudden death in preadolescents and adolescents. With an affected parent he should be screened now.

A 24-hour monitor done for an insurance physical shows premature ventricular contractions making up 0.5% of beats (about 700 per day). Ablation is for premature ventricular contraction-induced cardiomyopathy or for symptomatic low-risk patients who fail or cannot take drugs. Her low burden without symptoms needs reassurance and trigger removal.

An elevated B-type natriuretic peptide supports heart failure, but his 62 pg/mL is below 100 pg/mL, the cutoff used to rule it out. A normal result argues against a cardiac cause of his dyspnea.

After a week of colchicine therapy

Every three years is for a 3.0 to 3.9 cm aneurysm. His is 4.7 cm and growing rapidly, both well beyond that band; rapid growth is an indication for repair.

Her numbness extends above the toes over the dorsum of the foot, she has pain at rest, and toe and ankle movement are mildly weak. The arterial Doppler signal is inaudible, and the venous Doppler signal is audible. Which Rutherford class fits her limb?
opts: Class I, viable, has no sensory loss, no muscle weakness and audible arterial and venous Doppler signals. Her numbness beyond the toes, rest pain and weakness make her limb class IIB.

Class IIA, marginally threatened, has at most minimal sensory loss confined to the toes and no muscle weakness. Her numbness spreads above the toes with rest pain and mild weakness, which marks class IIB.

Correct. Sensory loss reaching beyond the toes with rest pain, plus mild-to-moderate muscle weakness, defines class IIB, immediately threatened: salvageable only with immediate revascularization. An inaudible arterial and audible venous Doppler signal fits that class, and atrial fibrillation is a classic cardiac source of the embolus.

Class III, irreversibly damaged, has profound sensory loss, paralysis and inaudible arterial AND venous Doppler signals. Her weakness is mild and her venous signal is still audible, so the limb is salvageable, class IIB.

opts: Endomyocardial biopsy is the gold standard that establishes myocarditis, but it is done once other causes of heart failure have been excluded. Coronary ischemia is excluded first, with cardiac angiography.
right test at the wrong stage

Correct. In suspected myocarditis, cardiac angiography is used to rule out coronary ischemia as the cause of new-onset heart failure. His diabetes and family history are cardiac risk factors, which makes ischemic disease a real alternative to exclude before the failure is blamed on his recent viral illness.

An erythrocyte sedimentation rate may be elevated in myocarditis as a nonspecific marker of inflammation. It cannot exclude coronary disease; cardiac angiography rules out ischemia as the cause of new heart failure.

Gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging shows the presence and extent of myocardial inflammation, supporting myocarditis. It is not the test used to exclude coronary ischemia; that is cardiac angiography.

Rate control is the first goal in atrial fibrillation, and stopping it before cardioversion has no basis. The step that must precede an outpatient cardioversion is 21 days of anticoagulation.

Immediate synchronized cardioversion is for hemodynamically UNSTABLE atrial fibrillation. She is stable and rate controlled, so an elective outpatient cardioversion waits until she has had 21 days of anticoagulation.

Correct. Outpatient cardioversion of atrial fibrillation is done only after 21 days of anticoagulation. She is stable and rate controlled, so there is no reason for an urgent shock, and she has had no anticoagulation yet.

ruled out by a stated finding

2.q: An 81-year-old man with atrial fibrillation, heart failure and chronic kidney disease is found at home with a cold left leg that has been painful for two days. The foot and calf have no sensation, he cannot move the ankle or toes, and the calf muscles are rigid. Neither arterial nor venous Doppler signals are audible. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Imaging such as computed tomography angiography fits viable or marginally threatened limbs, where there is time for it. Vascular imaging is generally not needed immediately for an irreversibly damaged limb, and decreased renal function is a contraindication to that contrast study anyway.
right test at the wrong stage

Immediate revascularization is what saves an immediately threatened limb, class IIB, with mild-to-moderate weakness. Paralysis, rigid muscles and silent arterial and venous Doppler signals mean irreversible damage, class III, which needs amputation.
right action at the wrong stage

Intra-arterial thrombolysis with alteplase is indicated for acute limb ischemia of less than 14 days in a limb that can still be saved. His limb is irreversibly damaged, class III, so restoring flow cannot rescue it and amputation is required.
right action at the wrong stage

Correct. Profound sensory loss, paralysis with rigid muscles and inaudible arterial and venous Doppler signals define an irreversibly ischemic limb, Rutherford class III. Major tissue loss or permanent nerve damage is inevitable, and a nonviable extremity requires major amputation regardless of the therapy instituted.

2.q: A 41-year-old woman had a ventricular septal defect repaired in childhood, with no residual defect. She now has a temperature of 38.3 °C (100.9 °F), and her long-known murmur sounds louder. One of three blood cultures grows coagulase-negative staphylococci. Transthoracic echocardiography shows no vegetation. How many modified Duke criteria does she meet?
opts: Three minor criteria would count her repaired septal defect and the single culture, but both are excluded: a repaired ventricular septal defect is not a predisposition, and one coagulase-negative staphylococcal culture is a likely contaminant. Only the fever counts.
ruled out by a stated finding

No major criterion is met: the louder old murmur does not count, the echocardiogram shows no vegetation and a single coagulase-negative staphylococcal culture is excluded. She has one minor criterion, the fever.
ruled out by a stated finding

This treats her louder murmur as new valvular regurgitation, a major criterion, but an increase or change in a preexisting murmur is not sufficient. With no major criterion, she has one minor: the fever.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Only her fever (38.0 °C or higher) counts, as one minor criterion. A repaired ventricular septal defect is excluded from predisposing conditions, an increase in a preexisting murmur is not sufficient for the major regurgitation criterion, and a single culture of coagulase-negative staphylococci is excluded as a common contaminant.

Her blood pressure is 84/52 mm Hg with pulsus paradoxus (a 10 mm Hg drop in blood pressure with inspiration), and her jugular venous pressure is elevated. Echocardiography shows a large effusion with right ventricular diastolic collapse. While pericardiocentesis is being arranged, which measure helps stabilize her?
opts: Correct. Pulsus paradoxus, hypotension, raised jugular pressure and right ventricular diastolic collapse are cardiac tamponade, for which expedient pericardiocentesis is definitive. Intravenous fluids are given meanwhile to increase preload and prevent collapse of the right ventricle, a temporizing measure.
Waiting a day ignores tamponade, an emergency with hypotension and right ventricular collapse. She needs intravenous fluids now as a bridge to expedient pericardiocentesis.

Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and colchicine treat acute pericarditis but do nothing to relieve a large effusion compressing the heart. She needs intravenous fluids to support preload until pericardiocentesis.
Furosemide removes fluid, the opposite of what tamponade needs: intravenous fluids are given to increase preload and keep the compressed right ventricle from collapsing until the fluid is drained.

opts: Observation suits blocks that are usually benign without symptoms, such as first-degree or Mobitz type I. Mobitz type II is considered dangerous even in the absence of symptoms, so he needs a permanent pacemaker.
Transcutaneous pacing is the EMERGENT treatment for an unstable Mobitz type II or complete block. He is stable, and the question is definitive management, which is a permanent pacemaker.

Correct. A constant PR interval with randomly dropped QRS complexes is second-degree Mobitz type II block, common with degenerative conduction disease of old age, hypertension and diabetes. It is considered dangerous even without symptoms because it can progress to complete block and sudden cardiac death; definitive treatment is a permanent pacemaker.
Waiting a year ignores the unpredictable progression of Mobitz type II to complete heart block and sudden cardiac death. The definitive treatment, even without symptoms, is a permanent pacemaker.

opts: Correct. Buttock and hip claudication with diminished femoral pulses and erectile dysfunction is the Leriche triad of aortoiliac disease. His diabetes, hypertension and smoking explain the atherosclerosis; the pain's location and the weak femoral pulses locate it.

Common femoral disease causes thigh claudication with NORMAL femoral pulses and decreased distal pulses. His buttock and hip pain, weak femoral pulses and erectile dysfunction place the disease higher, in the aortoiliac segment.
Tibial and peroneal artery disease causes foot claudication. Buttock and hip pain with diminished femoral pulses and erectile dysfunction comes from the aortoiliac segment.

Superficial femoral artery stenosis causes the most common pattern, claudication in the upper two-thirds of the calf. His pain is in the buttocks and hips with weak femoral pulses and erectile dysfunction, which is aortoiliac disease.

She has had a week of fatigue but is alert and afebrile, with a blood pressure of 118/70 mm Hg and a normal neurologic examination. opts: Late-stage infection is on the list of sinus bradycardia causes, but she is afebrile and her only complaint is fatigue. Her three rate-slowing medications are the documented cause; an infectious cause would come with fever and a source.
ruled out by a stated finding

Hypothyroidism is a listed cause of sinus bradycardia, but her thyroid-stimulating hormone of 2.1 sits inside the normal range, so it is not the cause here. Her three rate-slowing drugs explain the slow sinus rate; a thyroid cause would show an abnormal thyroid result.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. A regular rate of 46 with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS is sinus bradycardia, and beta blockers (metoprolol), nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (diltiazem) and digoxin are each a listed cause; she takes all three. Her normal thyroid result, normal neurologic examination and absent fever remove the thyroid, intracranial pressure and infection causes.

Increased intracranial pressure can slow the sinus node, but she is alert with a normal neurologic examination, so nothing points to it. The cause that fits her is the drug list: a beta blocker, a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker and digoxin together.
ruled out by a stated finding

opts: A temporary pacemaker is the SECOND step for unstable symptomatic sinus bradycardia, used when atropine does not work. With confusion and a pressure of 74/40, he gets atropine first, then temporary pacing if needed.
A permanent pacemaker is for chronic, symptomatic bradycardia, not the first move in an acute unstable presentation like his. The acute sequence is atropine first, then a temporary pacemaker.
No treatment is needed only when sinus bradycardia is asymptomatic. He is confused and hypotensive, which makes it acute, symptomatic and unstable, so atropine is given first rather than watching.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. This is sinus bradycardia (normal P before each narrow QRS, rate under 60) that is acute, symptomatic and hemodynamically unstable: he is confused with a pressure of 74/40. For that situation atropine is first line, then a temporary pacemaker, with a permanent pacemaker kept for chronic symptomatic disease.

opts: Correct. Empiric therapy, started only after blood cultures are drawn, covers staphylococci, streptococci and enterococci. For prosthetic valve endocarditis when the valve has been in place for 1 year or less, it is vancomycin plus gentamicin plus cefepime; his valve is 8 months old.
Penicillin G with gentamicin is a directed regimen for VIRIDANS STREPTOCOCCI once cultures identify them. Before results, an early prosthetic valve infection gets vancomycin, gentamicin and cefepime.

Nafcillin is directed therapy for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus once it is identified, and it would miss resistant staphylococci. Empiric therapy for a valve under 1 year old is vancomycin, gentamicin and cefepime.

Vancomycin plus ceftriaxone is the empiric regimen for native valve endocarditis, a subacute presentation, or a prosthetic valve in place MORE than 1 year. His valve is 8 months old, so he gets vancomycin, gentamicin and cefepime.

2.q: A 54-year-old woman with resistant hypertension has taken hydralazine for a year. She now has joint pains, pleuritic chest pain (sharp, worse with each breath in) and a pericardial friction rub (a superficial scratchy sound). Antinuclear antibody is positive, blood urea nitrogen is 14 mg/dL (normal 7-20), and she has had no tuberculosis exposure or recent viral illness. Which is the most likely cause of her pericarditis?
opts: Uremic pericarditis needs a blood urea nitrogen above 60 mg/dL; hers is 14. Hydralazine with joint pains and a positive antinuclear antibody points to drug-induced lupus.
ruled out by a stated finding
Tuberculosis is a cause of pericarditis especially in developing countries, but she has no exposure. A year of hydralazine with a positive antinuclear antibody fits drug-induced lupus.
ruled out by a stated finding
Most idiopathic pericarditis is likely viral, but she had no recent viral illness, and hydralazine with joint pains and a positive antinuclear antibody gives a specific cause: drug-induced lupus.

Correct. Drug-induced lupus from procainamide or hydralazine is a listed iatrogenic cause of pericarditis. A year of hydralazine, joint pains and a positive antinuclear antibody fit it, and her normal urea nitrogen and lack of tuberculosis exposure or viral illness make the other causes unlikely.

2.q: A 55-year-old man with hemochromatosis, diabetes and liver disease has progressive dyspnea, ascites and bilateral leg edema, with right-sided failure dominating. Echocardiography shows normal ventricular size and wall thickness, a preserved ejection fraction, abnormal diastolic function and markedly enlarged atria. Which cardiomyopathy is most likely?
opts: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy causes thick, often asymmetric septal walls of 1.5 cm or more with a small cavity, usually from an inherited sarcomere mutation. His walls are normal and his atria greatly enlarged from a storage disorder, the restrictive pattern.

Hemochromatosis can also appear in the workup of dilated cardiomyopathy, but that disease shows dilated, thin-walled chambers with a reduced ejection fraction. His normal-sized ventricles with a preserved ejection fraction and enlarged atria are the restrictive pattern.

Correct. Hemochromatosis is a storage disorder that deposits iron in heart tissue and causes restrictive cardiomyopathy: stiff ventricles of normal size with a preserved ejection fraction, abnormal diastolic filling and marked atrial enlargement, with right heart failure often more prominent.

Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is a transient systolic dysfunction of the apical and midsegments after an emotional or physical stressor, usually in postmenopausal women. His chronic diastolic failure from iron deposits is restrictive cardiomyopathy.

He now has sharp chest pain that is worse lying flat and eases when he leans forward, and a pericardial friction rub (a superficial scratchy or squeaking sound) is heard. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen and indomethacin are not given for post-infarction pericarditis, and glucocorticoids are also avoided, so aspirin is the anti-inflammatory; he is already in the aspirin-as-antiplatelet group in whom the others are avoided.

Ibuprofen is a first-line nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug for most acute idiopathic or viral pericarditis, but nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are not given for post-infarction pericarditis. Three days after his infarction, aspirin is the anti-inflammatory to use.

Indomethacin is listed with ibuprofen as a first-line nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug for most patients, but nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are avoided after a myocardial infarction. His pericarditis follows an infarction 3 days ago, so aspirin is used.

Prednisone is second-line therapy when nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are contraindicated, but glucocorticoid therapy is also avoided in peri-infarction pericarditis. Aspirin is the anti-inflammatory for pericarditis after an infarction.

right action at the wrong severity

Correct. right action at the wrong stage

Her electrocardiogram shows ST-segment elevation, troponin is elevated, and an echocardiogram shows hypokinesis of the apical and midsegments of the left ventricle. Which test confirms the diagnosis?
opts: Troponin is usually elevated in takotsubo cardiomyopathy as it is in a heart attack, and there are no reliable early differences between the two. Catheterization separates them, showing normal coronary arteries in most takotsubo cases.

Exercise echocardiography assesses functional capacity, exercise-induced ischemia and obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. A patient who may be having an acute coronary syndrome follows those protocols, and catheterization showing normal coronaries confirms takotsubo cardiomyopathy.

Endomyocardial biopsy is the gold standard for myocarditis, used once other causes of heart failure are excluded and the heart keeps deteriorating. Her stress-triggered syndrome is confirmed by catheterization showing normal coronaries.

Correct. Takotsubo cardiomyopathy mimics acute coronary syndrome, with ST elevation, raised troponin and apical and midsegment hypokinesis, after a stressor such as a loved one's death in a postmenopausal woman. Cardiac catheterization confirms it by showing, most often, normal coronary arteries.

He has an elevated jugular venous pressure that rises during inspiration (Kussmaul sign) and is scheduled for pericardiectomy. He asks what in his case most affects survival. Which feature is linked to the worst survival?
opts: Correct. Etiology is an important determinant of survival in constrictive pericarditis, and prior ionizing radiation is associated with the worst survival rates. Pericardiectomy still improves survival (5-year about 80%, 10-year about 60%), and earlier surgery has better outcomes.
Pericardial calcification is a highly specific but uncommon DIAGNOSTIC finding of constriction, not the survival marker. The cause linked to the worst survival is prior ionizing radiation.
More than half of constrictive pericarditis is idiopathic or viral, but those are not the causes with the worst survival. Prior ionizing radiation carries the worst survival rates.
Earlier intervention is associated with IMPROVED outcomes in those who need surgery, not worse ones. His radiation-related cause is the feature tied to the worst survival.

2.q: A 61-year-old man was treated for presumed heart failure with digoxin, and he also takes metoprolol, atorvastatin for hyperlipidemia and levothyroxine for hypothyroidism. An echocardiogram now shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy of 1.9 cm with a small left ventricular cavity and systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve (the anterior leaflet pulled into the outflow tract). Which medication should be stopped?
opts: Metoprolol should continue: a beta blocker is the initial medication for outflow tract obstruction, slowing the heart, improving diastolic filling and reducing contractility. Digoxin is the drug to stop.

Correct. The echocardiogram shows hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with obstruction: unexplained wall thickness of 1.5 cm or more, septal hypertrophy, a small cavity and systolic anterior motion. Digoxin is a positive inotrope, and positive inotropes are avoided because increased contractility raises the risk of myocardial ischemia and may induce arrhythmias.

Statins are not among the drugs to avoid in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Those are drugs that reduce preload or afterload, such as nitrates and diuretics, and positive inotropes such as digoxin, epinephrine and norepinephrine.

Levothyroxine treats his hypothyroidism and is not on the list of drugs to avoid in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The positive inotrope digoxin is, because increased contractility raises the risk of ischemia and arrhythmia.

His electrocardiogram shows a long-standing left bundle branch block (QRS 0.16 s, dominant S wave in V1, monophasic R waves in I, V5 and V6). Which treatment targets the block?
opts: Catheter ablation treats tachycardias and premature beats, and ablation can itself cause conduction block. Symptomatic left bundle branch block with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is treated with a biventricular pacer.

Correct. Left bundle branch block is usually left untreated, except when it is symptomatic with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, which calls for a biventricular pacer. His ejection fraction of 25% with exertional dyspnea fits that exception; dilated cardiomyopathy and hypertension are listed causes of the block.

Leaving the block untreated is right for an ASYMPTOMATIC left bundle branch block. He has symptoms with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, the exception that calls for a biventricular pacer.

Transcutaneous pacing is the emergent treatment for unstable Mobitz type II or complete block. His chronic, symptomatic left bundle branch block with a low ejection fraction calls for a biventricular pacer.

2.q: A 34-year-old woman with hypertension controlled on lisinopril has a prior electrocardiogram showing pre-excitation (a short PR interval with a delta wave, a slurred upstroke of the QRS). She now has palpitations. She is alert with a blood pressure of 124/76 mm Hg, and the monitor shows a fast, irregularly irregular rhythm with wide, varying QRS complexes: atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. Which drug is the right choice?
opts: Correct. Her old tracing shows pre-excitation (short PR, delta wave), so this irregular wide rhythm is atrial fibrillation over an accessory pathway. Atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White is treated with intravenous procainamide, never adenosine; she is stable, so no shock is needed, and ablation of the pathway is the later definitive step.

Adenosine is first line for ORTHODROMIC atrioventricular reentry, but it is never used for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White, which is what her irregular, wide, varying complexes show. The drug here is intravenous procainamide.

Ablation of the accessory pathway is the first-line CHRONIC management of Wolff-Parkinson-White, not the drug for the acute episode. Right now the irregular pre-excited rhythm is treated with intravenous procainamide.

Intravenous rate control fits stable atrial fibrillation with a rapid rate when there is NO accessory pathway. Her known pre-excitation makes this atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White, which is treated with intravenous procainamide.

2.q: A 70-year-old woman with osteoporosis and hypothyroidism develops chest pain and dyspnea in the hour after her house is destroyed by a hurricane. She has no hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia or smoking history. Her electrocardiogram shows ST-segment elevation, and her troponin is elevated. Which is the most appropriate initial management?
opts: Discharge is unsafe when ST elevation and raised troponin could be either takotsubo or a heart attack. She is admitted to cardiology and treated by acute coronary syndrome protocols until catheterization clarifies it.

Takotsubo is likely, yet nothing at the outset reliably separates it from acute coronary syndrome. Reassurance before catheterization could miss a true heart attack; she is managed by acute coronary syndrome protocols.

Endomyocardial biopsy is the gold standard for myocarditis, not the first step for a woman with ST elevation after a stressor. Takotsubo mimics acute coronary syndrome, so those protocols come first, and catheterization confirms the diagnosis.

Correct. Her picture suggests takotsubo cardiomyopathy, a postmenopausal woman with few cardiac risk factors after a natural disaster, but it mimics acute coronary syndrome with no initial reliable differences. Evaluation and treatment therefore follow established acute coronary syndrome protocols, with admission to cardiology.

2.q: A 64-year-old man has had poorly controlled hypertension for 25 years and also has chronic kidney disease. Echocardiography shows concentric left ventricular wall thickening of 1.6 cm. He has no family history of cardiomyopathy or sudden death. Which is the most likely explanation for the thickening?
opts: Correct. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is defined as left ventricular hypertrophy in the absence of a causative hemodynamic factor such as hypertension, and hypertensive heart disease is on its differential. Twenty-five years of poorly controlled hypertension explains his concentric thickening, even though it exceeds 1.5 cm.

Dilated cardiomyopathy shows dilated chambers with thin walls, and it is defined as occurring without hypertension or valve disease as the cause. His walls are thick, not thin, and his hypertension explains them.

Wall thickness of 1.5 cm or more confirms hypertrophic cardiomyopathy only when it is unexplained, and the definition excludes hypertrophy caused by hypertension. His long, poorly controlled hypertension explains it, and his thickening is concentric rather than the classic asymmetric septal pattern.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy has normal or only slightly thickened walls with markedly enlarged atria and impaired filling. Concentric thickening of 1.6 cm after decades of hypertension points to hypertensive heart disease.

2.q: A 70-year-old man with a history of kidney stones, hypertension and heavy smoking has sudden severe left flank and back pain. His blood pressure is 84/50 mm Hg, a pulsatile abdominal mass is palpable, and there is flank ecchymosis (Grey Turner sign). Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Renal colic is the classic misdiagnosis of a ruptured aneurysm, and his stone history makes it tempting. But a pulsatile abdominal mass is virtually diagnostic of rupture, and flank ecchymosis signals retroperitoneal hemorrhage.

Diverticulitis is another condition a ruptured aneurysm is often mistaken for. Hypotension with a pulsatile abdominal mass, which is virtually diagnostic, and flank ecchymosis from retroperitoneal hemorrhage point to rupture.

Ischemic bowel is also on the list of common misdiagnoses for a ruptured aneurysm. The pulsatile abdominal mass, hypotension and Grey Turner flank bruising identify retroperitoneal bleeding from a ruptured aneurysm.

Correct. Severe abdominal or back pain, a pulsatile abdominal mass and hypotension are the classic presentation of rupture, and the pulsatile mass is virtually diagnostic. Flank ecchymosis (Grey Turner sign) marks retroperitoneal hemorrhage; his kidney stone history is the trap, since rupture is often misdiagnosed as renal colic.

2.q: A 20-year-old man with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy plays competitive rugby, drinks heavily on weekends and often restricts fluids before games to make weight. He has no symptoms. Which counseling is most appropriate?
opts: Competitive, extreme exertion is what links hypertrophic cardiomyopathy to sudden cardiac death, especially in the young. Even without symptoms he is counseled toward mild-to-moderate noncompetitive activity.

Correct. Patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy have traditionally been told to keep to mild-to-moderate recreational activity in a noncompetitive way, because sudden cardiac death, the leading cause of death, is linked to extreme exertion. He should also stay hydrated and avoid excess alcohol.
Complete inactivity is not the advice; patients are guided to mild-to-moderate recreational activity done noncompetitively. The danger lies in extreme, competitive exertion, not in all movement.

Dehydration should be avoided in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, since less blood in the heart increases outflow obstruction. He should maintain hydration, not restrict fluids, and also cut back on alcohol.

Her temperature is 38.7 °C (101.7 °F), troponin is 0.12 ng/mL (normal under 0.04), and echocardiography shows a small effusion without tamponade. She takes no anticoagulant and has had no trauma. How many of the listed higher-risk features for acute pericarditis does she have?
opts: One counts only the fever. Immunosuppressive therapy and an elevated troponin are listed higher-risk features too, so she has three.
Two misses one item, usually the troponin: an elevated cardiac troponin suggests myopericarditis and is a listed higher-risk feature. Fever, immunosuppression and troponin make three.

Correct. Fever above 38 °C (1), immunosuppression (1) and an elevated troponin suggesting myopericarditis (1) are listed higher-risk features: 1 + 1 + 1 = 3. Her effusion is small (the feature is a MODERATE to large one), her onset was acute, and she has no anticoagulant or trauma. Any of these features points to possible hospitalization.
Four counts her small effusion, but the listed feature is a MODERATE to large effusion. Fever, immunosuppression and an elevated troponin make three.

2.q: A 68-year-old man with hypertension and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a 5.0 cm descending thoracic aortic aneurysm found on computed tomography. He has no chest or back pain, and the aneurysm has not grown over the past year. How often should it be imaged?
opts: Imaging every 3 to 5 years is the interval for a thoracic aneurysm smaller than 4.5 cm. At 5.0 cm his aneurysm sits in the 4.5 to 5.4 cm band, which needs imaging every 6 to 12 months.

Repair is generally indicated for a descending aneurysm larger than 6.0 cm, growth of more than 0.5 cm per year or any symptoms. His 5.0 cm aneurysm is stable and painless, so it is watched with imaging every 6 to 12 months.
right action at the wrong stage
Once found, a thoracic aneurysm is followed by size: under 4.5 cm every 3 to 5 years and 4.5 to 5.4 cm every 6 to 12 months. Stopping surveillance would miss the growth that changes management.

Correct. A 5.0 cm aneurysm of the descending thoracic aorta falls in the 4.5 to 5.4 cm band, imaged with computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging every 6 to 12 months. Repair is indicated for a descending aneurysm over 6.0 cm, growth over 0.5 cm per year or symptoms, and he has none.

2.q: A 48-year-old man with dilated cardiomyopathy drinks about 10 beers a day and also has hypertension and gastroesophageal reflux. His echocardiogram shows dilated, thin-walled ventricles with an ejection fraction of 25%, and he has started guideline-directed medications. Which counseling point offers the best chance that his heart function will improve?
opts: Sodium restriction to less than 2 g a day is standard education in dilated cardiomyopathy, but it does not remove the cause of his disease. Stopping alcohol, the offending source, is what can let his cardiac function recover.

Maintaining hydration and avoiding dehydration is advice for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, where less blood in the heart worsens outflow obstruction. His dilated, thin-walled heart from alcohol improves most when he stops drinking.

Correct. Long-term excess alcohol is a cause of dilated cardiomyopathy, and cardiac function can recover if alcohol intake is reduced or halted. Removing the offending source is the step most able to improve his heart, alongside his medications.

Genetic counseling is for patients with a family history of cardiomyopathy; familial disease causes up to 35% of cases. His history points to alcohol, the cause whose removal can let the heart recover.

2.q: A 52-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and breast cancer has a peripherally inserted central catheter in her left arm for chemotherapy. She now has a fever of 39.4°C (102.9°F), a tender, indurated cord along the arm vein, redness spreading well beyond the vein's margin and pus at the insertion site. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Superficial phlebitis is inflammation of the vein wall without a clot, so ultrasound shows wall thickening alone. Fever, pus and redness far beyond the vein point to infection within the vein, septic thrombophlebitis.

An upper-extremity deep vein thrombosis, usually from catheters or device leads, often presents only with limb swelling and arm discomfort. Her surface cord, high fever and pus localize to an infected superficial vein instead.

Superficial thrombophlebitis gives the same tender cord with redness and warmth over the vein, and a recent catheter is its most common upper-extremity cause. High fever, pus and redness far beyond the vein are what mark the septic form.

Correct. A tender, indurated cord along a superficial vein is thrombophlebitis; high fever, purulent drainage and redness extending well beyond the vein's margin point to infection within the vein. Septic thrombophlebitis is uncommon without venous cannulation, and her catheter supplies it.

2.q: A 68-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease (creatinine 2.4 mg/dL, normal 0.6-1.2) has uncomplicated native mitral valve endocarditis from viridans streptococci and is responding quickly to therapy. A short combination course is being discussed. Which drug should be left out because of her kidney disease?
opts: Ceftriaxone is a listed backbone for viridans streptococcal endocarditis and is not the drug her kidney disease rules out. The 2-week regimen's gentamicin is what requires the absence of chronic kidney disease.
Penicillin G is a listed agent for viridans streptococci and is not the one excluded by kidney disease. Gentamicin is: its 2-week combination is reserved for patients without chronic kidney disease.

Vancomycin is a listed alternative for viridans streptococci, not the drug named in the kidney-disease condition. The 2-week gentamicin regimen is the one limited to patients without chronic kidney disease.

Correct. For viridans streptococci, penicillin G or ceftriaxone can be given with gentamicin as a 2-week regimen, but only for uncomplicated endocarditis with a rapid response and NO chronic kidney disease. Her kidney disease rules out the gentamicin-containing short course.

His electrocardiogram shows flutter waves (a sawtooth pattern) with 2:1 block and a ventricular rate of 150. He is alert with a blood pressure of 128/80 mm Hg. This is his third episode despite rate control. Which offers definitive management?
opts: A pacemaker with a defibrillator is for tachy-brady syndrome whose fast rhythm is ventricular tachycardia. His problem is recurrent atrial flutter, which is treated definitively with ablation.

Correct. Sawtooth flutter waves with 2:1 block are atrial flutter, common after atrial scarring from surgery and in right-sided heart failure. He is stable, rate control is harder in flutter and recurrence is substantial, as his third episode shows; ablation is the definitive management, with anticoagulation alongside.

A beta blocker or calcium channel blocker is the stable-patient step, but rate control is harder to achieve in flutter and recurrence is substantial; this is already his third episode. Ablation is the definitive management.
Synchronized cardioversion is for HEMODYNAMICALLY UNSTABLE atrial flutter. He is alert with a pressure of 128/80, and the question is definitive management of recurrent flutter, which is ablation.

opts: Defibrillation (unsynchronized cardioversion) is for PULSELESS ventricular tachycardia, and for polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. She has a carotid pulse and identical complexes, so she gets synchronized cardioversion.
ruled out by a stated finding

Magnesium breaks torsades de pointes, a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with a long QT. Her complexes are identical (monomorphic) and she is unstable with a pulse, so synchronized cardioversion is next.

Lidocaine is pharmacologic cardioversion for STABLE monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. Her chest pain and pressure of 82/50 make her unstable, and with a pulse present she needs synchronized cardioversion.

Correct. Identical wide complexes at 190 are monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, and chest pain with hypotension makes it unstable. For unstable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia the next move is to check for a pulse: with a pulse present, synchronized cardioversion; without one, defibrillation.

2.q: A 71-year-old man who had infective endocarditis 2 years ago and has chronic kidney disease is scheduled for a screening colonoscopy. He has no active infection. Which is correct about endocarditis prophylaxis?
opts: Oral amoxicillin is the standard regimen when prophylaxis IS indicated, as before a dental extraction. Colonoscopy is a gastrointestinal procedure that does not require prophylaxis, even after prior endocarditis.

Parenteral ampicillin is for an indicated procedure when the patient cannot take pills. A screening colonoscopy is not an indication: gastrointestinal procedures do not require endocarditis prophylaxis.
Azithromycin is the oral choice for a penicillin-allergic patient having an indicated dental procedure. Colonoscopy does not require prophylaxis at all, whatever his allergy status.

Correct. Prior endocarditis puts him in a high-risk group, but prophylaxis is recommended only before dental procedures that manipulate the gums or tooth roots or perforate the oral mucosa, and invasive respiratory procedures. Gastrointestinal procedures such as colonoscopy do not need it in the absence of active infection.

2.q: A 58-year-old man treated for infective endocarditis 3 years ago now has a temperature of 38.9 °C (102.0 °F), conjunctival hemorrhages and Roth spots (white-centered retinal hemorrhages). One of three blood cultures grows viridans streptococci; the other two show no growth. Transesophageal echocardiography is normal. Which modified Duke classification fits?
opts: One major plus one minor would need a major criterion; his single positive culture is minor and his transesophageal study is normal. His five minor criteria make it definite.
Three minor criteria undercount him. Prior endocarditis, fever, conjunctival hemorrhages, Roth spots and the single positive culture are five minor criteria, and five minor make it definite.

Correct. Prior endocarditis (predisposition), fever, conjunctival hemorrhages (vascular), Roth spots (immunologic) and one positive culture that does not meet the major rule (microbiologic) are five minor criteria: 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 5, which defines definite endocarditis without any major criterion.

One major plus three minor treats his single positive culture as major, but the major culture criterion needs a typical organism from TWO separate cultures (or persistently positive cultures). One of three is a minor criterion.

Supine systolic pressures are: right arm 142 mm Hg, left arm 128 mm Hg; right ankle posterior tibial 92 and dorsalis pedis 86 mm Hg; left ankle posterior tibial 150 and dorsalis pedis 146 mm Hg. What is his overall ankle-brachial index?
opts: 0.61 divides the right dorsalis pedis pressure, 86, by 142. Each leg uses the higher of its two ankle pressures, here the posterior tibial 92, so the right index is 92/142 = 0.65, and that is the overall value.

Correct. Each leg's index is the higher of its two ankle pressures over the higher arm pressure: right 92/142 = 0.65, left 150/142 = 1.06. The lower of the two is the overall ankle-brachial index, 0.65, which sits in the claudication band of 0.4 to 0.9 and matches his calf pain with walking.

0.72 divides 92 by the left arm pressure of 128. The denominator is the higher arm pressure, 142 here, because the highest brachial reading is used; the right index is therefore 0.65, the overall value.
1.06 is his left leg, 150/142, which is normal. The overall ankle-brachial index is the LOWER of the two legs, so the diseased right leg's 0.65 is the number that counts.

2.q: A 64-year-old man with peripheral artery disease, type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease has sudden, tearing chest pain radiating to his back. Computed tomography confirms an aortic dissection. His blood pressure is 182/98 mm Hg. To what systolic range should his blood pressure be lowered now?
opts: 80 to 100 mm Hg is lower than the range set for acute dissection. The target is a systolic pressure of 100 to 120 mm Hg, reached with a beta blocker such as esmolol or a vasodilator such as nitroprusside.

Correct. Acute aortic dissection is managed by stopping its progression: lower the systolic pressure to 100 to 120 mm Hg with a beta blocker such as esmolol or a vasodilator such as nitroprusside, with pain control and surgery. That acute target is far lower than his long-term goal for diabetes and kidney disease.

Keeping him just under 130 borrows from the long-term goal of below 130/80 for peripheral artery disease with diabetes or renal failure. An acute dissection needs a lower systolic target, 100 to 120 mm Hg, to stop it progressing.
chronic goal applied to an emergency

130 to 140 echoes the routine peripheral artery disease goal of below 140/90. In acute aortic dissection the systolic pressure is brought down to 100 to 120 mm Hg with esmolol or nitroprusside to halt progression.

2.q: A 34-year-old man with type 1 diabetes and a 15-pack-year smoking history has a preoperative electrocardiogram showing prominent Q waves in leads II, III, aVF, I, aVL and V4 through V6 with left axis deviation. He has never had chest pain, and echocardiography shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy of 2.0 cm with normal wall motion. What best explains the Q waves?
opts: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy causes ST elevation and T-wave inversion with apical and midsegment hypokinesis after an emotional or physical stressor. He has no symptoms, no stressor and normal wall motion; his Q waves come from the thickened septum.

A silent infarction is tempting in a smoker with diabetes, but in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy prominent inferior and lateral Q waves reflect septal depolarization of hypertrophied tissue, and his echocardiogram shows a thick septum with normal wall motion.

Correct. In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy the electrocardiogram can show prominent Q waves in the inferior leads (II, III, aVF) and lateral leads (I, aVL, V4 to V6) with left axis deviation, reflecting septal depolarization of hypertrophied myopathic tissue. His 2.0 cm asymmetric septum explains them.

Left bundle branch block is a conduction delay listed among the electrocardiogram findings of dilated cardiomyopathy. Prominent inferior and lateral Q waves with a 2.0 cm septum are the hypertrophic pattern of septal depolarization.

2.q: A 56-year-old man with idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy has taken maximum medical therapy for 6 months, including an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor, a beta blocker and spironolactone. He also has type 2 diabetes and gout, and his electrocardiogram shows no heart block. His ejection fraction is now 25% (normal 50% to 75%). Which device is indicated?
opts: A permanent pacemaker treats conduction system disease, such as heart block from nodal fibrosis in restrictive cardiomyopathy. He has no heart block; his low ejection fraction after maximum therapy calls for a defibrillator against sudden death.

Medical therapy continues, but an ejection fraction still below 35% after maximum medical therapy is the indication for an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator. Without one he stays exposed to sudden cardiac death from arrhythmia.

A left ventricular assist device is bridge therapy to transplant or recovery, or destination therapy for patients who cannot have a transplant. His indication is an ejection fraction under 35% after maximum therapy, which calls for a defibrillator.

2.q: A 50-year-old woman with migraine and hypothyroidism has just flown overseas. She has sudden shortness of breath, pleuritic chest pain and a swollen, tender left calf. Her electrocardiogram, normal last year, now shows a new right bundle branch block: QRS 0.14 s with an rsR' pattern in V1 to V3 (bunny ears, a second upward deflection) and a slurred S wave in I and aVL. Which is the most likely cause of the new block?
opts: Correct. A wide QRS with an rsR' (bunny ears) in V1 to V3 is right bundle branch block, and a sudden rise in right ventricular pressure from pulmonary embolism is a listed cause. Sudden dyspnea and pleuritic pain after a long flight point to it, and the block was absent a year ago.

Degenerative change of the conduction system causes right bundle branch block that develops slowly with age. Hers appeared suddenly with dyspnea and pleuritic pain after a flight, which points to pulmonary embolism.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a listed cause of right bundle branch block, but it would not appear suddenly with pleuritic chest pain after a flight. A sudden right ventricular pressure rise from pulmonary embolism fits.

Lenègre-Lev disease (degenerative fibrotic conduction disease) is a listed cause of LEFT bundle branch block. Her new right bundle branch block with sudden dyspnea after a flight fits a pulmonary embolism.

2.q: A 52-year-old man develops chest pain, palpitations and new heart failure. He has had no recent viral illness, and coronary angiography is normal. He takes methyldopa for hypertension, metformin for type 2 diabetes, atorvastatin for hyperlipidemia and omeprazole for reflux. Myocarditis is suspected. Which of his medications is a recognized cause?
opts: Statins are not among the medications named as causes of myocarditis; that list includes penicillin, thiazide diuretics, tetracycline and methyldopa. His antihypertensive, methyldopa, is the one to suspect.

Correct. Methyldopa is among the medications that can cause myocarditis, along with penicillin, thiazide diuretics and tetracycline. With no viral prodrome and normal coronaries, a drug cause deserves attention.

Omeprazole does not appear among the medication causes of myocarditis, which include penicillin, thiazide diuretics, tetracycline and methyldopa. Methyldopa, his blood pressure drug, is the recognized culprit in his list.

Two points misses one item, usually the vascular disease point: a prior myocardial infarction counts there. Age (1), vascular disease (1) and hypertension (1) make 3.

Four points scores the myocardial infarction as 2, but among the history items only stroke, transient ischemic attack or thromboembolism count double; vascular disease is 1. His total is 3.

2.q: A 72-year-old man with atrial fibrillation is on hemodialysis for end-stage kidney disease, takes daily aspirin for a coronary stent and had a major gastrointestinal bleed last year. His blood pressure is 148/84 mm Hg. He has no liver disease, prior stroke or unstable international normalized ratio, and he drinks no alcohol. What is his HAS-BLED (bleeding risk) score?

Three points leaves out one of his four items, usually the aspirin, which counts as a medication predisposing to bleeding. Age, renal disease, prior bleeding and aspirin add up to 4.

Correct. Age over 65 scores 1, renal disease on dialysis 1, prior major bleeding 1 and aspirin (medication predisposing to bleeding) 1: 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4. 2.q: A 70-year-old woman with sepsis and ongoing gastrointestinal bleeding becomes unresponsive. The monitor shows an organized narrow-complex rhythm at 90 per minute, but no pulse can be felt. Which is the next step?
opts: Transcutaneous pacing treats unstable Mobitz type II or complete block in a patient who has a pulse. Pulseless electrical activity is a cardiac arrest rhythm treated with compressions and epinephrine.

Synchronized cardioversion is for unstable tachycardias WITH a pulse. She has no pulse with an organized rhythm, which is pulseless electrical activity, treated with chest compressions and epinephrine.

Correct. An organized rhythm that should produce a pulse but does not is pulseless electrical activity, and its two leading causes in adults are hypovolemia and hypoxia; bleeding makes hypovolemia likely here. It is unshockable: start chest compressions immediately, with epinephrine every 3 to 5 minutes.

Defibrillation treats ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia. Pulseless electrical activity, an organized rhythm without a pulse, is unshockable and needs chest compressions and epinephrine.

2.q: A 69-year-old woman with long-standing varicose veins of both legs comes to urgent care with swelling of her entire left leg for two days. She is receiving palliative treatment for metastatic breast cancer. Her left calf measures 2 cm more than the right, and she has no pitting edema and no tenderness along the deep veins. opts: A score of 1 drops her cancer because it is being palliated rather than cured. The Wells item reads treatment or palliation within 6 months, so her cancer earns 1 point alongside the swollen leg, for 2.

Correct. Active cancer, which includes palliation within 6 months, 1 + entire leg swollen 1 = 2, the moderate band. Her varicose veins do not score, because the item is collateral superficial veins that are nonvaricose, and a 2 cm calf difference falls short of the more-than-3 cm cutoff.

A score of 3 counts her varicose veins as collateral veins. The Wells item is collateral superficial veins that are nonvaricose, so long-standing varicose veins add nothing; cancer and the swollen leg give 2.

opts: Below 120/80 mm Hg is stricter than either goal set for peripheral artery disease. The goal is below 140/90, or below 130/80 for diabetes or renal failure, and her renal failure sets 130/80.

Correct. In peripheral artery disease the antihypertensive goal is below 140/90 mm Hg, tightened to below 130/80 mm Hg for patients with diabetes or renal failure. Her renal failure puts her on the stricter goal, so her current 146/88 needs more treatment.
Below 140/90 mm Hg is the general goal in peripheral artery disease, but it applies to patients without diabetes or renal failure. Her renal failure moves her to the stricter goal of below 130/80.

2.q: A 63-year-old man with a prosthetic aortic valve and type 2 diabetes has 10 days of malaise and fever to 38.8 °C (101.8 °F). Two separate blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. Transesophageal echocardiography shows an oscillating mass on the prosthetic valve. Which modified Duke classification fits?
opts: One major plus three minor is another route to definite endocarditis, but it miscounts him: both the cultures and the echocardiogram are MAJOR criteria, and he has only two minor ones (prosthetic valve, fever).

One major plus one minor criterion gives possible endocarditis. He has TWO major criteria, a typical organism in two separate cultures and an oscillating mass on echocardiography, which makes it definite.

Correct. Staphylococcus aureus, a typical organism, from two separate blood cultures is one major criterion, and an oscillating intracardiac mass on the valve is the second (evidence of endocardial involvement). Two major criteria define definite endocarditis; his prosthetic valve and fever are minor criteria that are not needed.
Three minor criteria alone give possible endocarditis, but his cultures and echocardiogram are major criteria, not minor ones. With two major criteria he is definite.

Two hours later the foot is cold and pale with absent pulses, numbness extends above the toes, and he has moderate weakness of ankle dorsiflexion. The arterial Doppler signal is inaudible; the venous signal is audible. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: There is time for imaging such as computed tomography angiography in a viable or marginally threatened limb. An immediately threatened limb with weakness should go straight to evaluation and treatment in the surgical suite.
right test at the wrong stage

Major amputation is for an irreversibly ischemic limb with profound sensory loss, paralysis and inaudible venous signals. His venous signal is audible and his weakness moderate, so the limb is still salvageable with immediate revascularization.
right action at the wrong stage

Intravenous heparin is the medical therapy for acute arterial occlusion, but observation wastes the window: an immediately threatened limb with weakness is salvageable only with immediate revascularization in the surgical suite.
right action at the wrong severity

Correct. Sensory loss beyond the toes with moderate weakness and an inaudible arterial but audible venous signal is Rutherford IIB, immediately threatened: salvageable only with immediate revascularization, so he should go to the surgical suite. opts: Correct. Revascularization is recommended for claudication with severe functional disability only after an inadequate response to exercise or drug therapy, and he has never tried exercise. A supervised program, more successful than a home program, of at least 30 to 45 minutes three times a week improves walking distance.

Percutaneous transluminal angioplasty is a minimally invasive revascularization, but revascularization is recommended only after exercise or drug therapy has failed. He has not yet tried an exercise program, so that comes first.
right action at the wrong stage

A bypass graft is invasive surgery used principally for severe critical leg ischemia. He has claudication without rest pain or ulcers and has not tried exercise therapy, so a supervised program comes first.

She is hemodynamically stable, has normal kidney function, has never had a bleeding problem and is reliable with follow-up. She also has treated hypothyroidism and takes an estrogen-containing contraceptive. Which finding makes outpatient treatment inappropriate?
opts: Correct. Outpatient therapy is not appropriate for an iliofemoral (proximal) deep vein thrombosis, even in a patient who is otherwise stable, at low bleeding risk, free of renal insufficiency and reliable. Her other features all fit outpatient care; the location of the clot is what sends her to inpatient treatment.

Estrogen therapy makes this a clot provoked by a minor transient risk factor, which sets treatment at 3 to 6 months. It shapes how long she is treated, not where; the iliofemoral clot is what rules out outpatient care.
Comorbidities exclude outpatient care only when they warrant inpatient care themselves, and treated hypothyroidism does not. The disqualifier is the iliofemoral, proximal extent of her clot.

2.q: A 58-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation has daily palpitations. Monitoring shows frequent premature atrial contractions (early, abnormally shaped P waves), and his atrial fibrillation episodes start right after runs of them. An echocardiogram shows no structural heart disease. He has cut out caffeine and alcohol, and three months of metoprolol has not helped. Which treatment fits best?
opts: Correct. Premature atrial contractions that persist with symptoms are treated with a beta blocker if not contraindicated, or with catheter ablation when they are frequent or are triggering atrial fibrillation. His are frequent, trigger his atrial fibrillation and did not respond to metoprolol, so ablation is the fit.

Frequent premature atrial contractions do call for a search for structural heart disease, but his echocardiogram has already shown none. The next step for persistent, triggering beats after failed metoprolol is catheter ablation.

Reassurance about the benign nature of premature atrial contractions fits patients without symptoms. His are frequent, symptomatic and set off atrial fibrillation, which is the indication for catheter ablation.

Synchronized cardioversion treats an unstable tachycardia, not isolated early beats. Frequent premature atrial contractions that trigger atrial fibrillation are treated with catheter ablation once a beta blocker has failed.

2.q: A 64-year-old man is admitted with a bleeding duodenal ulcer that is still oozing on endoscopy. On day 2 his right thigh swells, and duplex ultrasound shows a clot in the femoral vein. He also has hypertension and type 2 diabetes. Which is the most appropriate management of the clot?
opts: Rivaroxaban, a direct factor Xa inhibitor, is an oral anticoagulant and shares the same contraindication: active bleeding. With an ulcer still oozing, the femoral clot is managed with an inferior vena cava filter rather than any anticoagulant.
ruled out by a stated finding

Warm compresses and elevation treat superficial thrombophlebitis, a clot in a superficial vein that rarely embolizes. His clot is in the femoral vein, a proximal deep vein, and with active bleeding he needs a filter.

Correct. Active bleeding is a contraindication to anticoagulants. An inferior vena cava filter is used only when there is an acute proximal deep vein thrombosis of the leg, such as a femoral clot, together with active bleeding or another contraindication to anticoagulation, which is exactly his situation.

Enoxaparin, a low molecular weight heparin, is standard anticoagulation for deep vein thrombosis, but active bleeding is a listed contraindication to anticoagulants. His oozing ulcer rules it out, so a filter protects him instead.
